XVII.1.title: The pig from Yang Huo
XVII.1.reflection: Yang Huo, an upstart who had seized power in Lu, wants to see Confucius, who avoids him. Huo sends a roasted pig, so courtesy requires a visit of thanks; Confucius goes when Huo is out, and meets him on the road. Huo lectures him: can someone who hides his treasure and lets his state go astray be called ren? Or wise, if he loves office and keeps missing chances? The years do not wait. Very well, I will take office. A polite answer that commits him to nothing.
XVII.1.question: When have you agreed with someone just to end the conversation?

XVII.2.title: Near by nature
XVII.2.reflection: By nature people are close to each other; by practice they grow far apart. The only direct statement about human nature in the Analects, and it puts the weight on habit. The later debate about whether nature is good started from lines like this.
XVII.2.question: What habit has carried you furthest from where you began?

XVII.3.title: Only the highest and the lowest
XVII.3.reflection: Only the wisest and the most foolish do not change. Coming after XVII.2, it limits the claim: practice shapes almost everyone. The extremes are rare.
XVII.3.question: Do you believe you can still change in the ways that matter?

XVII.4.title: An ox-knife for a chicken
XVII.4.reflection: In Wucheng, where Ziyou governs, Confucius hears strings and singing, and smiles: why use an ox-knife to kill a chicken? Ziyou reminds him of his own teaching, that the governed learn the Way and become easy to lead. The Master tells the disciples Ziyou is right; he was only joking. The teacher is caught and admits it.
XVII.4.question: When were you caught by your own words, and how did you take it?

XVII.5.title: The invitation from Bi
XVII.5.reflection: Gongshan Furao, rebelling in Bi, invites Confucius, who is tempted. Zilu objects. Would he invite me for nothing? If someone used me, could I not make an Eastern Zhou? The book records the Master's eagerness to serve, even with dubious patrons.
XVII.5.question: What tempting offer have you considered from someone you did not trust?

XVII.6.title: Five things under Heaven
XVII.6.reflection: Zizhang asks about ren: practise five things everywhere. Respect, and you will not be insulted; generosity, and you will win people; good faith, and you will be trusted; diligence, and you will achieve; kindness, and you will be able to employ others. Each virtue is given its effect.
XVII.6.question: Which of the five would change most if you practised it more?

XVII.7.title: A gourd on a shelf
XVII.7.reflection: Bi Xi, rebelling in Zhongmou, invites the Master, and again Zilu objects with the Master's own words: the junzi does not join wrongdoers. True, I said so. But is it not said: what is truly hard can be ground and not worn thin; what is truly white can be dyed and not turn black? Am I a gourd to hang on a shelf and not be eaten? The desire to be used is stronger than the fear of being soiled.
XVII.7.question: When has wanting to be useful led you near something doubtful?

XVII.8.title: Six words, six blind spots
XVII.8.reflection: Zilu, have you heard of the six words and their six faults? Love of ren without love of learning becomes foolishness; of knowledge, dissipation; of good faith, harm; of straightness, harshness; of courage, disorder; of firmness, wildness. Every virtue needs learning to stay a virtue.
XVII.8.question: Which of your virtues most needs learning to keep it in shape?

XVII.9.title: Why study the Odes?
XVII.9.reflection: Why do you not study the Odes? They stir, they let you observe, they help you live with others, they let you voice complaint. At home they serve your father, abroad your lord, and they teach the names of birds, beasts, plants and trees. Poetry here is practical education.
XVII.9.question: What poem or song has taught you something about living with others?

XVII.10.title: Face to a wall
XVII.10.reflection: Confucius tells his son: have you studied the Zhounan and Shaonan, the first sections of the Odes? Not to study them is like standing with your face to a wall. Without them, one sees nothing ahead.
XVII.10.question: What book left you facing a wall when you did not know it?

XVII.11.title: More than jade and silk
XVII.11.reflection: Ritual, ritual, they say: is it just jade and silk? Music, music: is it just bells and drums? The gifts and the instruments are the outside of something else.
XVII.11.question: What ritual of yours has become only its outward things?

XVII.12.title: Stern outside, weak inside
XVII.12.reflection: A stern face over a weak interior is like a small man, a thief who breaks through walls. Pretended strength is a kind of theft, of a reputation not earned.
XVII.12.question: Where do you put on a firmness you do not have?

XVII.13.title: The village worthy
XVII.13.reflection: The village worthy is the thief of virtue. The one who pleases everyone and offends no one passes for good and blocks the real thing. Mencius later explains this saying at length.
XVII.13.question: Where are you agreeable when you should be good?

XVII.14.title: Passing it on
XVII.14.reflection: To pass on on the road what one heard on the road is to throw virtue away. Repeating what one has not made one's own, or spreading hearsay: both are meant.
XVII.14.question: What did you repeat today that you had only just heard?

XVII.15.title: Afraid of losing it
XVII.15.reflection: Petty men cannot serve a lord: before they have it, they worry how to get it; once they have it, they worry about losing it; and fearing to lose it, there is nothing they will not do. Office pursued for itself corrupts at every stage.
XVII.15.question: What would you be afraid to lose, and what might that fear make you do?

XVII.16.title: The old faults were better
XVII.16.reflection: People of old had three failings, and even those are gone: the old wildness was free, now it is reckless; the old pride was firm, now it is quarrelsome; the old foolishness was straight, now it is deceitful. Even the faults of the past were more honest.
XVII.16.question: Which of your faults is at least honest?

XVII.17.title: Fine words, once more
XVII.17.reflection: I.3 returns word for word. The repetition is itself a reminder that the book was gathered from several collections of sayings.
XVII.17.question: Have you noticed fine words more since you first read this?

XVII.18.title: Purple over vermilion
XVII.18.reflection: I hate purple taking the place of vermilion, the music of Zheng confusing the court music, and sharp tongues overturning states and families. Vermilion was a correct colour, purple a mixed one. Each line is about something that resembles the true thing and displaces it.
XVII.18.question: What imitation has displaced the real thing in your life?

XVII.19.title: Does Heaven speak?
XVII.19.reflection: I would rather not speak, says the Master. Zigong: then what will we disciples pass on? Does Heaven speak? The four seasons go round, the hundred things are born: does Heaven speak? Teaching without words, by being.
XVII.19.question: What have you learned from someone who never explained it?
XVII.19.exercise: Spend a few minutes in silence today and notice what goes on without anyone speaking.

XVII.20.title: The zither at the door
XVII.20.reflection: Ru Bei asks to see Confucius, who excuses himself as ill; as the messenger leaves, he takes up his zither and sings so that Ru Bei will hear. A refusal made plain without words. The reason is not given.
XVII.20.question: How do you refuse someone without saying no?

XVII.21.title: Three years in the arms
XVII.21.reflection: Zai Wo argues that a year of mourning is enough; three years would let ritual and music decay. Would you be at ease eating fine rice and wearing brocade after one year? I would. Then do it. When he leaves: Zai Wo is not ren. A child leaves its parents' arms only after three years; did Zai Wo not have three years of his parents' love? The argument from ritual is answered by an argument from feeling. This is one of the chapters a modern reader may find hard; it is here as the text gives it.
XVII.21.question: What do you owe to the years someone spent caring for you?

XVII.22.title: Better to play a game
XVII.22.reflection: To eat all day and set the mind on nothing is hard indeed. Are there not games of chance and board games? Even those would be better than doing nothing. An unexpected defence of play, against idleness.
XVII.22.question: What would occupy your mind better than idleness today?

XVII.23.title: Courage and rightness
XVII.23.reflection: Zilu asks whether the junzi values courage. He values rightness above all. A junzi with courage but no rightness causes disorder; a small man with courage but no rightness becomes a thief. Courage is a tool, rightness the aim.
XVII.23.question: When has your courage lacked rightness?

XVII.24.title: What the junzi hates
XVII.24.reflection: Zigong asks whether the junzi hates anything. Yes: those who spread others' faults, those below who slander those above, the brave without ritual, the bold who are narrow. And you, Ci? Zigong hates those who take snooping for wisdom, rudeness for courage, exposing secrets for honesty. Even dislike has its discipline.
XVII.24.question: What do you dislike, and does the dislike say something good about you?

XVII.25.title: Women and servants
XVII.25.reflection: Legge renders it: of all people, girls and servants are the most difficult to behave to; familiar, they lose their deference; distant, they resent it. The sentence speaks from inside a household where women and servants were placed below the master, and it says so without apology. The app keeps it in the cycle as the text has it, and the Lore article on hard passages explains why. Some readers take it narrowly, of concubines and household servants; that softens it only a little.
XVII.25.question: What does this sentence tell you about the household it describes?

XVII.26.title: Disliked at forty
XVII.26.reflection: Someone who is still disliked at forty will stay so to the end. IX.22 set forty as the age by which a person should be heard of. Here it is the age by which character is settled.
XVII.26.question: What in you is settled now, for better or worse?
